terms.p: An allocator that is one pointer moving forward through a fixed block of memory, so allocation is an add and there is no way to free a single object.
A linked list of the blocks an allocator has available, usually stored inside the free blocks themselves so the bookkeeping costs no extra memory.
One of a fixed set of block sizes an allocator rounds requests up to, so a request of a common size can be answered by popping a list instead of searching one.
The compiler's record of which allocated object a pointer is allowed to reach, carried along with the address and lost when the pointer is turned into an integer.
Merging two free blocks that end and begin at the same address into one larger block, so a later big request can be served.
Free memory that cannot be used because it is split into pieces smaller than the request, even though the total is large enough.
A lock that keeps re-testing an atomic flag instead of asking the operating system to sleep, which is right only when the section it guards is very short.
The property that no combination of safe calls to an API can cause undefined behaviour, no matter how wrong the caller is.
A block of memory that many objects are allocated from and that is freed all at once, rather than object by object.
